dsa-idx-154.explanation: Scanning by weight accepts 1-2 (1) and 2-0 (1), which already connects all three vertices with V-1 = 2 edges, so the heaviest edge 0-1 (10) is dropped — its endpoints share a DSU root by then and it would only close a cycle.

dsa-idx-161.explanation: There is exactly one way to make 0 — take no coins at all — which is why the DP seeds dp[0] = 1, the base case every larger amount is ultimately counted from.

dsa-idx-162.explanation: Taking items 0, 2 and 3 uses weight 1 + 4 + 5 = 10, exactly filling the knapsack for value 5 + 8 + 6 = 19.
Every item weighs more than the capacity 3, so nothing can be taken and the best value is 0.

dsa-idx-163.explanation: Because items may be reused, taking the weight-1 item eight times gives 8 x 2 = 16, beating two weight-4 items (14).
The only item weighs 5, which exceeds the capacity 2, so even unlimited copies cannot be used.

dsa-idx-164.explanation: Cutting the rod into two pieces of length 2 yields 5 + 5 = 10, which beats selling it whole (8) or as 1+3 (2 + 7 = 9).
A rod of length 1 cannot be cut any further, so the only option is to sell it whole for price[0] = 3.

dsa-idx-167.explanation: Deleting 'c' and 'd' leaves the palindrome "bb"; no palindromic subsequence of length 3 exists.

dsa-idx-168.explanation: Insert 'a' and 't' after the leading 's', then replace 'n' with 'r' to reach "saturday" in 3 operations.
Starting from an empty string the only option is inserting each of the 3 characters of the target.

dsa-idx-169.explanation: There are 5 distinct sets of positions in "babgbag" that spell "bag" in order.
The target is longer than the source, so no subsequence of s can equal t and the count is 0.

dsa-idx-170.explanation: The first '*' matches the empty sequence and the second '*' matches "dce", so the pattern consumes "adceb" exactly.

dsa-idx-172b.explanation: Each element divides the next, so the entire array is one divisible chain and nothing larger exists.
No two of these numbers divide one another, so the largest valid subset holds a single element (any one of them is accepted).

dsa-idx-173.explanation: The chain "xb" -> "xbc" -> "cxbc" -> "pcxbc" -> "pcxbcf" adds exactly one letter each step, giving length 5.
Neither word can be built from the other by inserting one letter, so the best chain is a single word.

dsa-idx-174.explanation: The whole array is already bitonic: it rises 1 < 2 < 5 and then falls 5 > 3 > 2.
A strictly increasing sequence counts as bitonic with an empty decreasing part, so all 3 elements are used.

dsa-idx-175.explanation: Multiplying left to right, ((A1 x A2) x A3) x A4 costs 1*2*3 + 1*3*4 + 1*4*3 = 6 + 12 + 12 = 30, the cheapest order.
The array describes a single 10x20 matrix, so there is nothing to multiply and the cost is 0.

dsa-idx-8.explanation: Transposing swaps 2 and 3, then reversing each row turns the square a quarter-turn clockwise: the left column [1,3] becomes the top row [3,1].

dsa-idx-10.explanation: Writing from the back, 2 is the larger tail so it takes the last slot, and the 1 already sits in its final place.

dsa-idx-30.explanation: With no pointer to the head, the node cannot be unlinked; instead it copies its successor's value over itself and skips that successor, which leaves the same visible list.

dsa-idx-114.explanation: The children already sum to 45, which exceeds the parent's 2, so the parent is lifted to 45 — values may only ever be increased.
The parent 50 outweighs its children's sum of 9, and values may only be raised, so both children are lifted to 50; the post-order pass then resets the parent to their new total, 100.

dsa-idx-123.explanation: The left child 2 is spliced in ahead of the right child 3, so the flattened right-spine reads 1 then 2 then 3, with every left pointer cleared.
With no left subtree anywhere there is nothing to splice, so the tree is already a right-leaning chain and is returned unchanged.
